entries.description: A ship-shaped vessel moored over an offshore field that receives well fluids, separates oil, gas and water, stores the oil in its hull and offloads it to shuttle tankers. Used where a pipeline to shore is impractical.
Stack of large valves on top of a well that can seal the wellbore and shut off uncontrolled flow of oil or gas during drilling. The last line of defence against a blowout.
Safety system that automatically or manually shuts down process equipment, isolates inventories and stops flow when a dangerous condition such as fire, gas leak or overpressure is detected.
Techniques used to recover oil that ordinary pressure depletion and water injection leave behind, such as gas injection, polymer flooding or CO2 injection. Also called tertiary recovery.
Natural gas cooled to about minus 162 degrees Celsius so it becomes liquid and shrinks to roughly 1/600 of its volume, making it practical to ship in tankers rather than by pipeline.

The seabed areas under Norwegian jurisdiction where petroleum activity takes place — the North Sea, the Norwegian Sea and the Barents Sea. The term the industry uses for the Norwegian offshore province as a whole.

The formal development plan an operator submits to Norwegian authorities for approval before building out a field — concept, facilities, cost, schedule and environmental impact. Approval is the go-ahead for the project.

The discipline and organisation responsible for protecting people and the environment in operations — risk assessment, incident reporting, procedures and safety culture. Sometimes extended to HSEQ with quality.

Two or more potentially conflicting activities carried out at the same time and place, such as drilling while producing or lifting near live process. Requires a dedicated risk assessment and coordination plan.
Detailed engineering drawing showing all pipes, valves, vessels, instruments and control loops in a process system. The primary reference document for operations, maintenance and modifications.
Wells or reservoirs with pressure above about 690 bar or temperature above about 150 degrees Celsius. They require special materials, equipment ratings and drilling practices.
Capturing CO2 from industrial or power sources, transporting it and injecting it into deep geological formations, often depleted reservoirs or saline aquifers, for permanent storage.
